Dengue: 5 more die, 1,366 hospitalized in 24hrs
item.description:
Five people died of dengue, and 1,366 new patients were hospitalized across the country in the 24 hours leading up to Tuesday morning.
With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll has risen to 357 in the country this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the new deaths, two were reported in the Dhaka North City Corporation area and Barisal division each and one was recorded in Rangpur division, it said.
Of the total fatalities, 53.1% were female and 46.9% were male.
Since January 1 this year, hospitals across the country have admitted 115,617 dengue patients. Of them, 109,316 have recovered.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,204 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Tuesday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,204.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,100, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
The three new suspected fatalities were reported across three divisions; Dhaka, Mymensingh, and Chittagong with one death each.
A total of 1,217 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Tuesday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 215,768.
During the same period, 42 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 23,199.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 191,761 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 184,168 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: 30 Bangladeshis return home after release from Cambodia detention centre
item.description:
Thirty Bangladeshi nationals who were released from an immigration detention centre in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, returned home on Tuesday.
They arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at around 12:15pm on a Thai Airways flight.
The returnees are Mohammad Harun Or Rashid, Mohammad Abdul Wadud, Mohammad Tarlib Hasan Titul, Sumit Chandra Das, Rakib Hossain, Bappi Das, Mohammad Labon Sheikh, Mohammad Abdur Rahman, Mohammad Billal Hossain, Mohammad Mostafa, Nur Nabi, Mohammad Emon Ali, Mohammad Barkatullah, Mohammad Rubel Mia, Ali Ahmed, Zahidul Islam, Shamsul Alam, Mohammad Abdur Rahman, Abu Jaher Sabuj, Shawon, Nahid Dhali, Raju Hossain, Mohammad Tayeb Ali Sheikh, Saimon Bhuiyan, Mohammad Rashedul, Mohammad Akash Ahmed, Mohammad Shimul Ali, Ashikur Rahman, Mohammad Alamin PK and Mohammad Kabir.
The Bangladeshis had travelled to Cambodia in search of jobs but became stranded at various scam centres in the country.
They registered to return home after the Cambodian government offered them the opportunity to leave without paying fines.
Accordingly, they arrived at Phnom Penh Airport on September 3. However, during immigration checks, Cambodian immigration police detained 32 Bangladeshis over various complications, including irregular immigration status.
Two were subsequently released, while the remaining 30 were held at the immigration detention centre.
Following an application by an organization named Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation, the first secretary of the labour wing at the Bangladesh Embassy in Bangkok was asked to take the necessary steps to secure the detainees’ release and facilitate their early return home.
After the required procedures were completed in phases, the 30 Bangladeshis returned to Bangladesh on Tuesday.

item.title: India’s Russian oil in focus as Rubio visits major Reliance refinery
item.description:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.
Rubio’s business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India’s purchases of Russian oil.
Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it’s a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India’s energy relationship with Russia.
In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.
US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.
Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India’s continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.
In February 2026, Trump announced a “trade deal” that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.
While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India’s deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India’s top supplier of crude oil.
In mid-September, Trump signed the “Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act,” imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India.
However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions.
Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the “C5+1” diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.
“We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries,” he said.
“We’re trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We’re very close to doing that,” Rubio added.
In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.
Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
He said Jamnagar is an “important node in global trade” because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.
Although Trump’s sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.
Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio’s decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.
“The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar,” she told DW. “The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue.”
Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.
Shankar pointed to Reliance’s proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is “one of the states in play” in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.
“Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome,” she said.
The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defense, trade, technology and energy.
Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.
“Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values,” he said.
The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.
Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.
On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (Perm) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.
The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.
Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump’s own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.
“Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians,” Pant told DW.
Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump’s presidency.
“The sense that America is unreliable, that America can’t be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse,” he said.
The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.
“If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals “will have consequences.”

item.title: UN: More than 250,000 displaced within Yemen since fighting flared
item.description:
More than 250,000 people have been internally displaced in Yemen since the civil war reignited, the United Nations said Tuesday.
Yemen’s civil war -- in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis -- reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.
After an uneasy, four-year truce, Yemen’s conflict has surged back to life and then intensified when the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Displacement is continuing to rise sharply across Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, which was already suffering a vast humanitarian crisis.
“UNHCR is obviously deeply concerned about the escalating displacement situation,” Matthew Saltmarsh, spokesman for the UN refugee agency, told a press conference in Geneva.
“The numbers displaced have now reached over 250,000.
“These are people who have been internally displaced in Yemen between August 1 and October 17.”
Around half of those newly displaced are being hosted in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognized government.
“The most immediate needs that we’ve been able to identify are around shelter, food, and multi-purpose cash assistance, said Saltmarsh.
The spokesman noted that as of Saturday, some 3,836 new arrivals had been recorded in Djibouti, and a further 242 in Somalia, including both refugees and returnees.
Following the capsizing of a boat travelling from Djibouti to Yemen on the night of October 8-9, 139 bodies have been recovered, including 109 who have been identified, he said.
Meanwhile 82 survivors have been identified and were receiving support.

item.title: UN says 19m Afghans facing acute food insecurity by April
item.description:
The number of people facing acute food insecurity in Afghanistan is set to rise to 19.2 million during the winter season between November and April, the United Nations said Tuesday.
The food crisis in Afghanistan is projected to affect millions of children in 2027, the UN humanitarian agency Ocha said.
Between September and October, 15.9 million people -- or nearly one in three Afghans -- were facing food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, including 3.4 million in emergency conditions, the agency said.
But the outlook is set to deteriorate further.
“The number facing acute food insecurity is projected to rise to 19.2 million, of which five million are expected to face emergency levels of hunger,” which is “one step away from famine,” said Ocha’s Afghanistan spokeswoman Olga Cherevko.
The food crisis in Afghanistan is not simply about whether the food is available, but also about whether people can afford it, she told a press briefing in Geneva, speaking from Kabul.
The latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification snapshot projects that more than four million children aged six months to five years old will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year.
“Over one million of these children are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition,” said Cherevko.
“These numbers represent children whose parents cannot afford nutritious food, and families whose ability to cope has been worn down by years of conflict, economic hardship, drought and other shocks.”
However, around one-third of nutrition sites across the country have closed or have suspended services, “largely due to funding cuts.”
“Once these services disappear, the consequences could be irreversible, particularly for children.”

item.title: Saudi says intercepted Houthi missile, blasts heard in capital
item.description:
Saudi forces on Tuesday said they had intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom’s capital, after authorities issued a danger warning and AFP journalists reported hearing blasts.
The kingdom “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh,” said Turki Al-Malki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition backing Yemen’s government in its war against the Houthis.
Riyadh was shaken by two blasts, according to AFP journalists in the capital.
“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert for a potential danger,” the Saudi civil defense said in a statement on X.
But the alert was lifted a few minutes later, with the civil defense saying “the danger has passed.”
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have reached an unprecedented scale, forcing the postponement of a major investment conference in a blow to Riyadh’s hopes of attracting greater foreign capital and diversifying its economy.
The deadly attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis have forced Riyadh airport to shut.
The Saudi air force has been regularly targeting the group in retaliation amid fighting inside Yemen between the Houthis and the country’s Riyadh-backed government.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh’s control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before uprooting Yemeni government forces from positions along the Red Sea coastline in a lightning campaign in September.

item.title: Salesforce is planning to buy AI marketing company Braze, sending BRZE shares surging 50%
item.description:
A move announced by the software-as-a-service giant Salesforce (NYSE: CRM) is sending the stock price of a relatively unknown AI marketing firm surging this morning. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

On Tuesday morning, Salesforce announced plans to acquire digital marketing firm Braze (Nasdaq: BRZE) for about $5.66 billion. According to the terms of the deal, Salesforce will pay Braze Class A common stockholders $47.50 in cash per share. 

Braze’s AI-powered multichannel marketing solutions will be integrated into Salesforce’s core offerings, which Salesforce believes will give it an edge with its enterprise solutions.

This is especially true at a time when Wall Street has become concerned about a so-called SaaSpocalypse. Business models of legacy software-as-a-service companies are feared to be under threat as businesses increasingly turn to AI solutions to meet their needs.

“AI is raising the bar for marketers, who now need agentic solutions that can understand customers, make decisions, and act in real time,” Salesforce noted in a release announcing the news, adding that “Braze’s real-time engagement and AI decisioning capabilities are expected to complement all four layers of Salesforce’s architecture — Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and SIForce.”

What is Braze?

While even those outside the tech industry have likely heard of Salesforce, Braze is a much smaller and lesser-known company.

It is headquartered in New York and was originally founded in 2011. Its primary focus is as a multichannel marketing provider for enterprise customers to help them better understand and interact with their consumers.

Braze allows companies to interact with their customers across multiple channels, including WhatsApp, email, mobile websites, and more. In recent years, the company has shifted to AI offerings to better help clients engage with their customers.

Braze currently says it has around 2,770 customers, which include Venmo, Dairy Queen, Instacart, Canva, and more.

The company was private for the first decade of its existence, but went public in 2021 on the Nasdaq.

Braze shares skyrocket 50% 

Salesforce’s offer price of $5.66 billion for Braze equates to about a 58% premium over what the company was valued at as of market close yesterday, when BRZE shares closed just above $30.

Given that premium, it’s no wonder that BRZE skyrocketed right after the deal was announced. Currently, as of the time of this writing, BRZE shares are up more than 50% to $45.33 per share. That’s just a little more than $2 below what Salesforce says it will pay for the company.

Still, the stock’s current price is a far cry from its 2021 post-IPO highs.

Shortly after Braze went public, its shares traded at almost $100 per share at one point, according to Yahoo Finance data. But since then—even with today’s 50% gains—BRZE shares have fallen by around 48%.

Of course, while Salesforce has announced its intentions to buy the company, no deal of this size is certain until regulators have signed off and money has actually exchanged hands. And that won’t be during Salesforce’s current fiscal year.

Salesforce says the deal is expected to close during the company’s 2028 fiscal year, which runs from February 1, 2027, to January 31, 2028. It did not give an indication of when during that fiscal year the sale would close.

item.title: America's Counter-Drone Authority Is Real, The Capacity Isn't Yet
item.description:
Here is a number worth sitting with: federal teams seized roughly 700 drones around World Cup venues this summer. Seven hundred — at one tournament, in one season, with the best-resourced counter-drone units in the world on the field. That figure is a success story and a warning in the same breath: the threat volume is enormous, and the federal government cannot be the only team suiting up for it.

Until this year, it legally had to be. The power to disable a hostile drone belonged to a short list of federal agencies, which left a state trooper at a stadium gate or a corrections captain watching an aircraft hover over his yard with nothing but binoculars and a report form. Congress ended that with the SAFER SKIES Act in December's defense bill, and the DHS-Justice framework implementing it has been in force since July 1: state, local, tribal, and territorial police and corrections agencies that complete federal training and certification, on approved equipment, can now track a threatening drone and — against a credible threat — take it out of the sky above major venues, critical infrastructure, and prisons.

And in the past week, Washington has shown it means to deliver. The Justice Department announced that the FBI's counter-drone training center in Huntsville will double its capacity. DHS's Science and Technology Directorate put commercial counter-drone systems through operational testing alongside state and local officers. The Pentagon selected four directed-energy systems for a homeland counter-drone pilot. This is what implementation momentum looks like, and the departments deserve real credit for it.

Now the hard truth: doubling a small number produces a small number. The Huntsville center's first class, last fall, held twelve officers, and it remains the only place in America where a state or local officer can earn the legal right to bring down a drone. More than 18,500 agencies are now eligible for these authorities. Against that denominator, even a doubled schoolhouse leaves the vast majority of American communities exactly where they were — watching — while the Super Bowl arrives in four months and the Los Angeles Olympics in under two years. Our prisons cannot wait either: drone incidents at federal correctional facilities rose twentyfold in six years, and state systems from South Carolina to Georgia are logging airborne contraband runs by the hundreds.

What turns momentum into coverage is money, sustained past the current news cycle. Congress should fund training at the scale of the authority it created: regional and satellite course delivery so a deputy in Phoenix is not waiting on a classroom seat in Alabama, instructor pipelines that multiply the schoolhouse instead of merely enlarging it, and a certification target tied to the event calendar that oversight committees actually track. Just as important, the FEMA counter-UAS grant program — $500 million across 2026 and 2027, built around the World Cup — should not sunset with the tournament that inspired it. The threat is not leaving when the fans do.

Governors have their own homework, and fewer excuses than ever: the grant rules push at least 97 percent of awarded funds down to local and tribal agencies within 45 days. The money is designed to reach the street. States should name a lead agency, compete for those dollars this cycle, and put their corrections systems and stadium districts first in line for certified teams.

Over more than twenty years in federal homeland security — the last of them leading U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — I watched threats outrun statutes again and again. This time the statute arrived first, and this past week proved the executive branch intends to use it. The remaining question belongs to Congress and fifty governors: whether a nation that just confiscated 700 drones at a single sporting event will fund protection for everyone else. Authority without capacity is a promise. Appropriations are how promises get kept.

History may not be about to repeat itself in Serbia, but it is beginning to rhyme. Just over a quarter of a century ago, Serbian citizens turned out to vote in large numbers to inflict a historic defeat on the then strongman in Belgrade, Slobodan Milošević, who was seeking re-election as president. He lost despite his extensive control over the media, the judiciary and the security forces. When he was reluctant to leave office, Serbs poured on to the streets in their hundreds of thousands, finally forcing him to go.

On Sunday, a new generation could have the decisive voice in an equally fateful election, this time for the national parliament. Today’s strongman, Aleksandar Vučić, recently resigned as president to fight the election with the aim of swapping the locus of power from the presidency to the prime minister’s office.

item.title: Australian fast bowler Megan Schutt suspended over medication breach
item.description:
Star Australian fast bowler Megan Schutt was suspended for two matches on Thursday for breaching prescription medication rules.

The 33-year-old, who was a standout in Australia’s recent one-day series against Bangladesh, apologised for “failing to meet the standards” expected of her.

Cricket Australia said in a statement she breached “requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication”.

“This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance enhancing purposes,” it added.

“We will continue to provide appropriate support to Megan and reinforce the standards and responsibilities expected of everyone representing our game.” Her two-match ban will see Schutt miss Thursday’s third and final T20 against New Zealand and the Adelaide Strikers’ opening game of the Women’s Big Bash League later this month.

“I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me,” said Schutt, who has played 114 ODIs and 126 T20s for Australia.

“I’m sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I’ve received.”

item.title: Trump says he wants Zelensky to “make a deal” with Russia
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday urged Volodymyr Zelensky to make a deal with Russia -- redoubling pressure on the Ukrainian leader even as Moscow grinds on with the war it launched four years ago.

Trump also said he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Stephen Hubbard -- an American taken captive by Moscow's forces years earlier in Ukraine -- in a fresh sign of his pivot back to Moscow.

"We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," Trump told reporters in the same room.

Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Zelensky had a bruising televised confrontation in the Oval Office in February 2025, shortly after the Ukraine-skeptic US president returned to office.

"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump said Tuesday.

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Putin and slammed Zelensky as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

The Ukrainian leader met Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday for talks aimed at easing the tensions.

Zelensky hailed the resumption of US intelligence sharing on looming Russian strikes, but insisted Kyiv must be included in any future talks on its fate after meetings with US envoys.

Ukraine has been increasingly alarmed by Trump's return to effectively blaming Kyiv for a failure to end the war that began with Moscow's February 2022 invasion, and by his warm words towards Putin.

Trump indicated that a deal with Russia to free Hubbard could be near.

"I've been talking to President Putin about Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said in response to a question from an AFP journalist.

"Just stick with me," Trump added. "Just you remember that question a couple of days from now, because I do things that nobody else can do."

Trump confirms US-India trade deal finalisation soon
item.description:
US President Donald Trump has echoed Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicating that the bilateral trade agreement with India was close.

Speaking at a news briefing on Tuesday (local time), Trump was asked if the trade deal with India was close.

The US President replied, " They want to make a deal. We're going to make a deal. Pretty close, yeah. Going to be a much different kind of a deal than we've made in the past."

Earlier, Rubio revealed that the India-US trade deal is “incredibly close”, indicating that finalisation is anticipated shortly.

Speaking to Network18, Rubio noted that while he is not directly engaged in the negotiations, which are handled through the trade representative, he has closely monitored the discussions and expects the agreement to materialise in a matter of weeks, not months.

“I’m not personally negotiating it; it’s done through our trade representative, but I know, and I’ve been very involved in watching it happen, that it is something we anticipate seeing in a matter of weeks, not months,” said Rubio.

Elaborating on the meticulous final stages, he highlighted the necessity of absolute precision prior to public announcements to safeguard bilateral ties of such high importance.

“I felt that way before, and with these deals, it’s always important that it would be totally agreed to, every detail of it, before it’s announced because you can’t afford for a relationship of this magnitude to be threatened by announcing a deal and it turning out the deal wasn’t finalised. But it’s incredibly close. I think we are down to some technical details that need to be worked out. Technical details matter because there has to be an agreement; both sides have to agree that the language means the same thing. So, it’s down to that level,” he said.

Addressing queries concerning comparative rates for India alongside other nations, Rubio affirmed that the overarching outcome remains highly advantageous.

“The preponderance of it is good for you. And that’s what we aim to achieve here, and I can’t wait till we do it because we have so many things we can work together on,” Rubio stated.

Commenting on the sheer magnitude and diversity of the nation, the US Secretary of State underscored the necessity of broad exploratory visits rather than confining diplomatic engagements strictly to capitals.

“Well, this is a big country, it’s an important country, and I think like any big country, I say, people, if you want to learn and see what’s happening in the United States, you can’t just go to Washington. You should probably try to go somewhere in the South, maybe somewhere on the West Coast, and you probably need to get to New York, in Chicago. And so, for us, I mean, I don’t pretend that in my time as a Secretary of State I’ll get to see all of India, or learn about every region, but I think it’s important to see a country of this size and magnitude and to learn as much about it as you can,” Rubio remarked.

The India–U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement marks a major milestone in India’s global trade engagement, securing sustained preferential access for Indian exports in the U.S. market valued at over $30 trillion.

The agreement delivers comprehensive tariff rationalisation, zero-duty access across large product categories, enhanced digital and technology cooperation, and a carefully calibrated framework to safeguard India’s farmers, MSMEs and domestic industry.

item.title: Recruitment for 100,000 third and fourth class govt posts stalls
item.description:
Proposals to recruit staff for around 100,000 temporary posts in grades 16 to 20 across various government offices have been left pending.

Ministries and divisions cannot recruit for these third- and fourth-class positions because of revisions to the outsourcing policy. As a result, they cannot hire staff despite the demand, leaving members of the public deprived of essential services.

Until now, government offices recruited third- and fourth-class employees through outsourcing agencies or private companies. Under the revised policy, however, they can no longer recruit through private companies.

Ministries, divisions and government offices can recruit staff directly. Alternatively, a ministry or division may recruit through the Infrastructure Investment Facilitation Company (IIFC), a specialised organisation approved by the Finance Division.

The problem arose from the revision of the Service Procurement through Outsourcing Process Policy, 2025. The Ministry of Finance issued the policy on 21 September.

The revised policy allows government offices to obtain services directly from individuals instead of engaging private companies to provide outsourced services.

However, the Public Procurement Act and Rules contain no provision for procuring such services directly from individuals. Nor do the Public Procurement Rules (PPR) specify how ministries can directly recruit temporary staff for grades 16 to 20. Consequently, legal complications have emerged in implementing the new policy.

Since the revised policy came into force, various ministries and divisions have been unable to recruit third- and fourth-class employees through service-providing companies. At the same time, they cannot recruit the staff directly either.

Officials from various government departments and people familiar with the sector consider the policy incomplete and flawed. They say it does not clarify what will happen to ongoing tender processes for hiring staff through service-providing companies. Several ministries have written to the Ministry of Finance seeking a clear explanation of the matter.

Asib Ahsan, joint secretary of the Health Education and Family Welfare Division, told Prothom Alo that the division had asked the Ministry of Finance how it should handle ongoing tenders. His division plans to recruit several thousand service workers on a daily-wage basis. However, the lack of clarity in the policy has prevented it from proceeding with these appointments.

Since the revised policy came into force, various ministries and divisions have been unable to recruit third- and fourth-class employees through service-providing companies.

At the same time, they cannot recruit the staff directly either. In response to this situation, the Finance Division has written to the Bangladesh Public Procurement Authority (BPPA), requesting the necessary amendments to the Public Procurement Act and Rules. The Finance Division sent the letter on 21 September.

Recruitment stalls across various ministries

According to relevant sources at the Ministry of Finance, the new policy has stalled proposals to recruit staff for temporary posts under various ministries and divisions. These positions include hospital cleaners, laboratory assistants, trolley attendants and other service workers. The proposals also cover recruitment for cleaning and other support services at government residences and offices.

The revised policy allows government offices to obtain services directly from individuals instead of engaging private companies to provide outsourced services. However, the Public Procurement Act and Rules contain no provision for procuring such services directly from individuals. Nor do the Public Procurement Rules (PPR) specify how ministries can directly recruit temporary staff for grades 16 to 20.

Various institutions under the Ministry of Health have proposed recruiting around 20,000 service workers. Meanwhile, the Public Works Department plans to recruit around 5,000 employees to maintain government residences and offices. However, the new policy has prevented these recruitment processes from moving forward.

Relevant sources said similar situations had arisen in the Ministry of Railways, the Ministry of Social Welfare, the Ministry of Agriculture and several other ministries. Overall, recruitment proposals for around 100,000 temporary posts in grades 16 to 20 remain pending.

What is the Finance Division proposing?

In a letter dated 21 September, the Finance Division stated that it had revised the Service Procurement through Outsourcing Process Policy, 2025 to improve efficiency in government operations, ensure services are delivered in the shortest possible time, strengthen transparency and accountability, reduce public expenditure and procure quality services.

The letter stated that the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and the Public Procurement Rules, 2025, classify outsourcing as a physical service. However, neither the Act nor the Rules covers the procurement of such services directly from individuals.

The Finance Division therefore asked the Bangladesh Public Procurement Authority (BPPA) to take the necessary steps to incorporate provisions allowing the direct procurement of outsourced services from individuals into the Public Procurement Act and Rules, so that the revised policy could be implemented.

BPPA’s observations

In response to the Finance Division’s letter, the BPPA reviewed the proposal to procure outsourced services directly from individuals, along with the amendments the Finance Division had made to the policy.

In a letter to the Ministry of Finance dated 14 October, the authority stated that one of the main objectives of introducing outsourcing was to avoid direct contractual relationships between government offices and service workers.

Another objective was to prevent the financial and administrative complications that could arise if these workers later demanded inclusion in the government’s revenue budget.

Under the current system, the procuring authority signs a contract with a service provider selected through a competitive process. The service workers then provide services at government offices as employees of that company. However, allowing government offices to enter into contracts directly with individuals would fundamentally change the outsourcing framework. This could lead to the re-emergence of the complications that the existing system was designed to avoid.

The BPPA also noted that many individual service workers might lack the expertise required to follow and fulfil the prescribed contractual arrangements for providing services under the legal framework governing public procurement. As a result, implementing contracts directly with individuals could prove difficult.

The authority further warned that excluding private service providers could adversely affect the existing service sector. It could also raise questions about equal participation in public procurement.

The BPPA’s observations noted that barring private-sector participation in any government procurement process could conflict with the legal framework governing public procurement and international practices.

In addition, Rule 99(1)(b) of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025, requires government-owned entities that provide physical services through direct contracts to deliver those services using their own personnel.

Therefore, the authority believes that the government should also consider the staffing levels, institutional capacity and potential conflicts of interest of the relevant public-sector organisations when assessing their ability to provide outsourced services nationwide.

The BPPA’s letter stated that the government should also review the methods used to select service workers, contractual liabilities and private-sector participation in a coordinated manner. The authority has therefore requested discussions involving the Finance Division, the BPPA and relevant stakeholders to determine the next steps.

2 opposing views on outsourcing

Opinions differ on whether government offices should recruit staff in grades 16 to 20 through private companies. Temporary employees recruited through private firms allege that they have to pay substantial sums to service providers before securing jobs in government offices.

Even after they start working, the companies deduct a portion of their monthly salaries. Describing the practice as a form of slavery, these workers have been demanding that the government recruit them directly.

Owners of private companies, however, argue that private recruitment allows them to train employees before assigning them to work. They also hold the workers accountable if any untoward incident occurs.

They contend that the government lacks the capacity to provide such training if it recruits employees directly. They also argue that holding workers accountable would be difficult if an untoward incident occurred under direct government recruitment.

Abu Taleb, president of the Bangladesh Outsourcing Manpower Provider Society, told Prothom Alo that private companies had recruited more than 500,000 workers for government institutions. He said the service providers were responsible for training, monitoring and ensuring accountability among these employees before and after recruitment.

The government now wants to recruit third- and fourth-class employees directly, he said, adding that this would increase disorder in government operations.

He also believes that direct recruitment would lead to more irregularities and corruption among government officials. Moreover, government institutions lack the capacity to recruit such a large workforce.

Why outsourcing recruitment was introduced

Sources at the Ministry of Finance said the government first introduced an outsourcing policy in 2008. At the time, the government argued that expenditure on salaries, allowances and pensions for public officials and employees was increasing and needed to be reduced.

To cut spending on various allowances and pensions, the government began recruiting workers for third- and fourth-class positions on a temporary basis from 2009, rather than appointing them directly to permanent government posts.

The policy stipulated that government authorities could not enter into contracts with individuals when procuring outsourced services. Instead, they had to sign contracts with recognised private companies. Authorities were also prohibited from issuing appointment letters in the names of individual workers.

The government subsequently revised the policy twice more, in 2018 and 2025.

Uzbekistan keen to expand multifaceted partnership with Bangladesh
item.description:
Uzbekistan has expressed readiness to further expand the multifaceted partnership with Bangladesh, one of South Asia’s rapidly developing countries.
President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev received President of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh Dr Khalilur Rahman, on Tuesday.
Both sides reaffirmed their shared interest in further developing constructive cooperation on achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, advancing regional cooperation in Central Asia, addressing the impacts of climate change, and promoting a culture of peace and interfaith dialogue, according to the Uzbekistan President’s office.
Dr Khalilur arrived in Uzbekistan to attend the World Summit on “Investing in Children’s Well-being: Towards Sustainable and Equitable Development for Future Generations”, scheduled to take place in Samarkand on October 21-22.
At the beginning of the meeting, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev warmly congratulated Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, noting that Uzbekistan was the first country he had visited in this capacity.
Khalilur Rahman, in turn, conveyed warm greetings from UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to the President of Uzbekistan.
The discussions focused on further expanding and strengthening cooperation with the United Nations and its agencies.
In recent years, the UN General Assembly has adopted 15 resolutions initiated by Uzbekistan, including two approved this year.
Uzbekistan actively participates in the work of the UN’s principal organs and bodies. The country has also announced its candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2035–2036 term.

item.title: Death toll from Sudan army strike in disputed territory rises to 153
item.description:
The death toll from a drone strike Monday on a market in an area disputed between Sudan and South Sudan has risen to 153 and is likely even higher, a local official told AFP on Wednesday.
Authorities in Abyei district said the strike on the Amiet market involved the use of multiple munitions and was carried out by the Sudanese army.
“The number of casualties is 153 and it may increase any time from now because some victims burned to ashes and the rescuers are doing their best to gather all the bodies in Amiet Market,” said Yohana Akol, interim information minister for Abyei Special Administrative Area.
He said the victims included Sudanese, South Sudanese, Ethiopians and Somalis, and a further 19 have been hospitalized, with more on the way.
Images shared with AFP showed bombed-out buildings and vehicles.
“A swarm of drones was hovering over the Amiet Market and they bombed part of the market and surroundings and there were so many casualties,” a witness told AFP by phone, speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“Some of business places are still on fire and there were people burned beyond recognition inside,” the witness added.
Another witness said fuel depots were severely damaged.
On Sunday and Monday, strikes across Sudan killed more than 100 people. The country is in the grips of a brutal war between the regular army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that began in April 2023.
Abyei district is claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan, which split from its northern neighbor in 2011 following decades of conflict.
Parts of the district are controlled by a faction of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), a splinter from the organization that fought for Juba’s independence.
Juba’s foreign ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador over the attack, which it condemned “in the strongest terms possible.”
The United Nations also condemned the attacks, saying escalating drone strikes were “part of a deeply concerning pattern.”

item.title: Chattogram hosts final of next year’s Women’s U19 T20 World Cup
item.description:
Bangladesh will play the United Arab Emirates in Sylhet on the opening day of the ICC Women’s U19 T20 World Cup, which Bangladesh and Nepal will co-host from January 21 next year.
The International Cricket Council released the full schedule on Wednesday. The final will be played in Chattogram on February 6, and the city will also host both semi-finals on February 4.
Only the semi-finals and the final have reserve days.
The tournament will be played at four venues, two in each country. Sylhet and Chattogram will stage 12 matches each, while Mulpani will host eight and Kirtipur seven. The two Nepal grounds will hold group matches and some Super Six games.
Eight teams will be in action on the opening day, with two matches each in Sylhet and Mulpani. Play will start at 9:30am and 1:30pm local time.
Bangladesh are in Group C with Australia, the UAE and Nigeria, and will play all three group matches in Sylhet. After facing the UAE, they meet Australia on January 23 and Nigeria on January 25.
Two-time champions India are in Group A with Ireland, Nepal and West Indies. Pakistan will take on New Zealand, Samoa and South Africa in Group B, while the USA, Scotland, England and Sri Lanka make up Group D.
The group stage ends on January 26. The top three teams from each group go through to the Super Six, where qualifiers from Groups A and D form one group and those from Groups B and C the other.
Each team plays two Super Six matches, and the top two from each group reach the semi-finals.
India won the inaugural edition in South Africa in 2023, beating England in the final, and kept the title in Malaysia in 2025 with a win over South Africa.
Bangladesh reached the Super Six in both editions but have never played in a semi-final.

item.title: The UN’s latest climate change report is spotlighting the U.S., and not for a good reason
item.description:
Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.

“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.

The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries’ climate fighting plans. He wasn’t part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound.

Shooting far past Paris climate goal

The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection.

Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.

The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”

Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.

“The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn’t part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”

An added tenth of a degree of danger

Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.

“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”

Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.

And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.

“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

item.title: BBC layoffs: More jobs slashed, channels cut as British broadcaster faces ‘immediate cost pressures’
item.description:
Media companies continue to struggle as consumers pivot away from traditional forms of content. 

The latest example comes from the BBC, which has announced it will cut over 100 jobs. The U.K.-based broadcaster is attempting to save £500 million ($670 million) over the next two years. 

BBC is primarily funded by a licensing fee, a £180 annual payment that provides viewers with all TV channels, streaming services, and more. It’s designed to keep the BBC “free of advertisements and independent of shareholder and political interest” in the U.K. 

However, the number of TV licenses sold has shrunk in recent years. 

“We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world,” BBC director-general Matt Brittin said in a statement. “We all know that means tough choices.” 

Channels and archive radio network cut

In pursuit of this mission, the BBC will also stop broadcasting BBC Scotland and BBC Three, a channel geared toward younger audiences, come spring. It’s further cutting archive radio network Radio 4 Extra, with its content available on the BBC Sounds app. 

“Axing these TV channels and Radio 4 Extra may make business sense in a world where audiences are increasingly finding their BBC content on-demand, but I understand it saves less than 10 million pounds a year, a tiny fraction of what’s needed,” BBC News culture and media editor Katie Razzall said in a broadcast. “So far, the BBC has announced 200 million pounds in savings; it needs to find another 300 million pounds more.” 

The BBC plans to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs over the next couple years. It already slashed 550 positions in June. 

“There is a bigger fight going on here,” Razzall elaborated in an article. “The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future—and how it will be paid for. It won’t harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient.” 

Rachel Jupp, director of BBC News, will be announcing more savings plans in early 2027. 

Reached for comment, a BBC spokesperson referred Fast Company to its press release about the latest cuts.

BBC Three commissioned popular shows such as Fleabag, Killing Eve, and Normal People. Despite cutting its broadcast, the BBC Three team is receiving more money for commissions targeting audiences aged 16 to 34. 

BBC Scotland and BBC Three will be available on BBC iPlayer, the company’s online streamer, along with other platforms such as YouTube. BBC Scotland’s programs will also air on BBC One or BBC Two in the country, but the channel’s nightly News at Seven will stop running. According to the BBC, 12% of Scots watched BBC Scotland last year.

item.title: Netflix’s stock just collapsed to a 2-year low: Is the streaming giant’s ad business in trouble?
item.description:
Shares in Netflix Inc. (Nasdaq: NFLX) have fallen to a more than a two-year low after the streaming giant posted its Q3 2026 results yesterday.

Despite hitting Wall Street’s projected revenue target of nearly $12.9 billion for the quarter, an update on the company’s increasingly critical ad business dampened investor optimism, sinking the stock with it. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

Yesterday, Netflix announced its results for its third quarter of fiscal 2026. Unfortunately for the company, those results—and Netflix’s guidance—were somewhat of a mixed bag.

There was good news: Revenue for the quarter totaled $12.87 billion, representing 11.8% year-over-year growth.

The company’s diluted earnings per share also reached 87 cents. As noted by CNBC, this means Netflix hit the revenue target investors were expecting and exceeded EPS expectations by five cents per share.

However, there was also plenty of news that gave investors pause—and that has caused the stock to drop significantly in premarket trading today.

What did Netflix project?

For the fourth quarter, Netflix said it expects revenue to grow by about 11.5% to $13.44 billion. Double-digit growth is nothing to sneeze at, but unfortunately for Netflix, that revenue forecast comes in under the $13.51 billion that Wall Street was expecting, notes TipRanks. 

When it comes to its full fiscal 2026 guidance, Netflix says it now expects revenue of $51.1 billion. As with its Q4 forecast, that is a double-digit increase (about 13% year over year), but it is also on the lower end of the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range Netflix previously forecast for fiscal 2026.

But perhaps what spooked investors most of all was the updated guidance for Netflix’s ad business. The company said it now expects full-year 2026 ad revenue to be around $2.7 billion. That’s $300 million, or 10% less, than the $3 billion in ad revenue Netflix had previously forecast.

What’s weighing on Netflix’s ad business?

As most Netflix subscribers will have noticed, the company has been raising prices on its ad-free subscriptions for years. But Netflix isn’t stupid. It knows that price rises mean consumers’ pocketbooks will be hit harder.

However, Netflix also believes that by jacking up ad-free subscription costs, it will cause many cost-conscious consumers not to cancel their subscriptions, but instead to opt for lower-cost, ad-supported tiers.

While these lower-priced subscriptions mean Netflix will extract less up-front revenue from subscribers, over the long run, Netflix should make more money from each subscriber by serving them ads.

Netflix isn’t alone in this. Nearly every major streaming service has introduced ad-supported tiers in recent years in hopes of transitioning more users to them in order to boost their bottom lines.

In the industry, ad-supported subscriptions are seen as a way for streamers to boost revenue. Investors, too, have put significant hopes for revenue growth into ad-supported tiers.

That’s why investors were so disheartened to hear Netflix announce that its total full-year 2026 ad revenue is expected to come in 10% lower than previously forecast. 

As for one of the primary causes of the ad forecast reduction, Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said it was due to a slower launch of some ad products than originally expected.

“[S]pecifically in this case, we’ve seen some delays in the rollout and partner integrations for some of those new ads products,” Peters said on the company’s financial call, according to a PitchBook transcript. “So getting to the integration model that we want sometimes takes a bit more work with our partners, but we strongly believe that a modest short-term hit for a better long-term strategic position is a good ultimate tradeoff.”

Peters added that the slower rollout shouldn’t impact long-term gains, but investors tend to think in quarters, not the long term. And the lower ad forecast helped drive Netflix stock lower as well.

How have NFLX shares reacted?

As of the time of this writing, NFLX shares are down more than 6.4% to $64.23 in premarket trading. That’s after the company’s shares closed down 1.66% yesterday to $68.69.

Netflix’s current premarket price of around $64 per share is an ignominious milestone for the company. Its share price has not been that low since August 2024—more than two years ago. 

Even before today’s 6.4% drop, Netflix’s stock price was trading down more than 26% for the year.

Over the past year, the stock’s price has declined a staggering 44.5% as of yesterday’s close, according to data from Yahoo Finance.

Where the stock goes next is anyone’s guess, but investors will clearly be keeping an eye on the company’s ad efforts in the quarters ahead—efforts Peters seems to have faith in.

“[U]ltimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that’s a big mechanism of growth for us,” he told analysts on yesterday’s call. “So we are very focused on getting those out to them as quickly as we possibly can.”

Correction: Netflix’s previous 2026 guidance was in the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range, not $15.0 to $15.4 billion range as an earlier version of this article stated.

The outcome of the battle for Donbas — and the war itself — hinges on whether Ukraine can hold Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. How are two former Azov commanders leading the defense?
item.description: The Ukrainian command is trying to stop the Russian offensive — the decisive push in the battle for Donbas — on the approaches to the Kramatorsk-Sloviansk urban area. To do this, it has created two operational groupings, both led by veterans of the Azov Brigade: the “Center” grouping, tasked with holding Sloviansk, is commanded by Andriy Biletsky (former commander of the 3rd Army Corps), while the Azov grouping guarding the approaches to Kramatorsk is commanded by Denys Prokopenko (former commander of the 12th National Guard Brigade, which was reconstituted after the 2022 capture of its forces in Mariupol in 2022). Biletsky’s troops have already distinguished themselves with a successful offensive: they pushed Russia’s 20th Army back across the Siverskyi Donets north of Sloviansk, and are now trying to drive back the forces advancing on the city from the east and south. Prokopenko’s task is harder: he took up his new post in the midst of a fresh Russian breakthrough between Dobropillia and Kramatorsk. In this sector, Ukrainian forces are dealing with a full-blown crisis — possibly more serious than the one caused by the Russian breakthrough in the same area 14 months ago. Russian troops have already cut the Dobropillia-Kramatorsk road, are storming the first city, and are pushing toward the outskirts of the second.

item.title: Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030?
item.description:
Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030? Expert comment thilton.drupal 22 October 2026

Egyptian president’s surprise announcement comes amid deep economic difficulties and includes a plan for a military-approved succession.

Egypt’s President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi has declared he will step down at the end of his third term in 2030. Speaking during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation on 17 October, he also outlined a military-centric succession process to select the next president and senior officials beyond 2030. 

The statement surprised many observers, and perhaps even state officials. If Sisi follows through on his pledge and leaves peacefully, he’d be the first Egyptian president to leave office without dying, being imprisoned or facing a popular uprising. 

The unprecedented decision will have significant implications for Egypt’s political landscape, the balance of power within the regime and the military’s influence over politics and governance.

Why is Sisi leaving?

Sisi became president in 2014, after the overthrow of Mohamed Morsi’s short-lived Muslim Brotherhood government. He is currently serving his third term, after winning elections seen as predetermined in 2018 and 2023. A constitutional referendum in 2019, also seen as predetermined, increased the president’s term from four to six years, extending Sisi’s current term to 2030.

Sisi, who is 71, did not give an exact reason for why he would step down in his speech at the military academy. He said that there would be no further amendments to Egypt’s constitution to prolong his rule and declared it ‘a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed,’ suggesting a transition of power is inevitable.  

Economic troubles

Two factors likely lie behind this surprise decision. 

First, the debt-financed economic model pursued under Sisi is unsustainable. This system has sustained military dominance and stalled urgent economic reform. The government’s vast borrowing to fund mega projects has created a structural economic crisis. 

In this year’s budget, debt servicing accounts for 63.9 per cent of planned expenditure, a significant increase from 43 per cent in 2014. Interest payments alone, as a share of GDP, exceed the combined allocations for education, healthcare, wages and subsidies combined. Egypt’s external debt rose from $46.1 billion in 2014 (16.4 per cent of GDP) to $164.8 billion (38.9 per cent of GDP) by the end of Q1 2026. 

The Egyptian pound exchange rate has plummeted from 7.14 per dollar in mid-2014 to about 53.8 per dollar in October 2026. Urban inflation has risen from 8.3 per cent in May 2014 to 13.9 per cent in September 2026 and is expected to rise further. 

This increased pressure on ordinary Egyptians has made the last decade one of plummeting living standards. Official data shows the national poverty rate has reached 35.7 per cent in 2023.

Public anger over rising living costs, combined with structural imbalances and rising debt, have made Sisi’s economic policies untenable – even among his allies.

The long-lasting economic crisis is an existential threat to the regime’s stability. Sisi himself may have calculated that Egypt urgently needs a new social contract to avoid economic-driven social unrest that could push him out or plunge the country into perpetual chaos. 

He will likely want to avoid the fate of President Hosni Mubarak, who was forced to leave office amid the January 25 Revolution in 2011. It is also likely that there will be an arrangement to protect Sisi and his family members from potential future prosecutions as a condition of him stepping down. 

Protecting the state 

The second factor relates to Sisi’s vision for his presidency and the state. This is fundamentally shaped by the 2011 uprising, which he has described as ‘the death certificate of the Egyptian state.’ 

Since he was sworn in in 2014, Sisi has repeatedly warned that another popular uprising would threaten the state’s existence. He has portrayed national prosperity as depending on excluding from Egypt’s politics what he frequently calls ‘ahl elshar’ (people of evil), often understood as referring to Islamists. He has also warned of threats to ‘national memory’ on social media. 

Sisi has portrayed it as his – and the military’s – national duty to spare Egypt the chaos engulfing other Arab Spring countries by removing the Muslim Brotherhood from power amid a popular uprising. He has indicated that he considers it his duty to reshape Egypt’s politics to guarantee long-term stability as he sees it.   

In his speech at the military academy, Sisi revealed that he had insisted on incorporating Article 200 into the 2019 constitutional amendments. This article effectively designates the military as the guardian of Egypt’s national, secular identity and the regime. 

Given this, Sisi may therefore feel that departing in 2030 is in line with his aims. The military-trained officials he has designated as his successors would serve as the practical implementers of this vision.

Military-shaped succession

Alongside his plans to step down, Sisi also announced that the armed forces will fund a 30-month military academy course to train potential future leaders. Egyptians will then be able to ‘elect and choose’ from among the graduates.

The course will train select candidates, who must have a PhD and be 40-50 years old, for positions including minister, member of parliament, governor, and potentially even president. Those who have served in government for at least six years will be exempted. 

Sisi’s choice of the military academy is not surprising, since it has long been tasked with promoting a military-centric nationalism and overseeing appointments and promotions in state institutions. This has sometimes sparked resistance, for example from judges in January. 

In effect, the system will replace the electoral process with competence criteria, narrowing the pool of trusted candidates and excluding anyone who is ‘tendentious, a traitor, or a criminal’ from becoming president. 

Future implications

Although this process finally paves the way for civilians to become president, the military will likely retain decisive influence over leadership selection and the state’s strategic direction. The military’s constitutional mandate means its commanders’ views and preferences would continue to shape key state decisions.

Related work

Should Egypt join the Mecca Pact?

In this setup, Sisi will likely retain entrenched loyalties and broader political influence. The changes could establish an informal military guardianship model that sits above the president and government beyond 2030. This might resemble Turkey in the 1990s.

The new government training system might also invite challenges. It seems designed to side-line dissidents, the Muslim Brotherhood and rival generals. But by effectively excluding individuals without a postgraduate degree or those who fail to secure academy approval, it might be deemed unconstitutional and face legal challenges. It could also spark fierce competition among key security branches.

Will Sisi reconsider?

Sisi’s decision to step down might face resistance from key institutions and influential figures in his patronage system, who may try to convince him to reconsider to protect their interests. 

These attempts may intensify if Egypt’s military becomes involved in escalating regional conflicts. Sisi recently sought authorization from parliament to deploy troops to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. 

If living conditions worsen and social unrest breaks out, Sisi may conclude that staying in power best guarantees stability for Egypt. 

Potential for civilian rule?

Despite its risks, Sisi’s decision may facilitate a transition towards a less authoritarian government in the long term. It took Egyptians 15 years after the 2011 uprising to hear an Egyptian president pledge an ordinary, peaceful transition of power. 

By declaring he will step down, Sisi could end up kickstarting a tradition in which no single ruler stays in power until death. Civilians might finally be seen as capable rulers. 

This will not happen overnight, of course. It would depend on Sisi keeping his word and social stability holding until 2030. But if this is the case, the military guardianship Sisi is establishing may, in the long term, be seen as a transitional period toward a more stable, more open and freer society.

item.title: Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine?
item.description:
Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine? Expert comment jon.wallace 22 October 2026

Not immediately. But a Democratic victory could set the terms for a new approach by the next president.

Whatever the results, November’s midterm elections will not immediately transform US policy toward Israel and Palestine. In any outcome, the separation of powers means that President Donald Trump will still control American foreign policy. Even a Democrat-controlled Congress could not compel his administration to pursue a fundamentally different approach. 

But the midterms may accelerate a transformation that is already underway in the Democratic Party and among the US electorate, where the political centre of gravity on Israel and Palestine is shifting rapidly. 

If Democrats win a majority in either or both houses, they will gain new congressional tools to act on Israel–Palestine issues. Most importantly, the legislation they put forward would establish the policy baseline from which a future Democratic administration would govern.

The shift

Among dozens of others, Democrats like Abdul El-Sayed, running for the US Senate in Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres, running in the general against another Democrat in California, have drawn considerable attention for their criticism of Israeli government actions – and US support for them. The race in Michigan, which could be decisive for Democratic hopes to retake the senate, looks tight.

But even if progressive candidates don’t do as well as expected in these elections, a shift is underway. Developments in Washington over just the past month illustrate how much has already changed.

On 29 September, 46 of 47 Senate Democrats voted for a resolution led by Senators Chris Van Hollen, Tim Kaine and Bernie Sanders. This would ‘require the Department of State to provide information and assessments related to investigations of the killing of United States citizens by violent Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces in the West Bank’. The resolution did not pass the Republican majority. But the vote was remarkable for its unanimity. Such Democratic unity on a resolution critical of Israel would have been almost unimaginable only a few years ago.

The vote follows a distinct trajectory in Democratic politics. When Senator Bernie Sanders forced the Senate to vote on blocking weapon sales to Israel in November 2024, only 18 Democrat senators supported him. This April, 40 of 47 Senate Democrats voted against a sale of bulldozers to Israel. And 36 opposed the sale of 1,000-pound bombs. Now, with the September resolution, virtually the entire Senate Democratic caucus has voted to demand accountability from Israel.
